maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION

speechtext:
Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of
Justice) moved:
That the special committee appointed to study the Dominion Elections Act, 1934, and amendments thereto, and the Dominion Franchise Act, 1934, and amendments thereto, be instructed to study and make report on the methods used to effect a redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and in other countries, and to make suggestions to the house in connection therewith.
He said: When the motion to appoint a committee to consider the elections act and the franchise act was before the house, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) asked whether the committee would deal with the recent redistribution of seats in this house, I replied in the negative. Since then notice of motion has been given to appoint another committee for that purpose. The motion I now present to the house would meet neither the views of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, nor the object of the resolution on the order paper. Its aim is rather to study, in a strictly non-partisan, non-political way, methods which could be adopted with regard to redistributing seats in Canada when the necessity arises.
When the last redistribution bill was before the house the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) expressed the view that instead of redistribution being proceeded with by a committee of the house, necessarily composed of a majority representing one of the political parties, it ought to be possible to find a way to have this work done by an independent tribunal, either a royal commission or some other board, which would give some guarantee of impartiality. In the end the redistribution was voted by the majority against the protests of the minority in the house, and there has remained in many quarters, I am free to say, a sense of injustice as to what was done in certain parts of the country. This motion would empower the committee to study the methods used in other places situated similarly to our own country. For instance, in the sister dominion of Australia, a growing country in which the population increases from one census to another,
Elections and Franchise

they have a method under which redistribution is brought about by a board composed of three officers, one of whom is the chief electoral officer and another the surveyor general. Their report is submitted to the parliament of Australia, but if the recommendations contained in the report are not considered proper in every respect it is not necessarily adopted. At all events it seems to me that we have here something which ought to appeal to the sense of impartiality of every hon. member. The motion will not commit parliament to anything, it will simply give the committee authority to study the question and to report to the house as to what in the opinion of the committee would be the proper system of redistributing the representation of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not certain that this is not a motion which should be preceded by notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext: It was.

maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
Oh, I understand. The
question which arises on the motion may be said to divide itself into two branches, the first of which is covered by the constitution. Section 51 of the British North America Act reads as follows:
On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time, as the parliament _ of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules:
(1)	Quebec shall have the fixed number of sixty-five members:
(2)	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained):
(3)	In the computation of the number of members for a province a fractional part not exceeding one-half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded'; but a fractional part exceeding one-half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole number:
(4)	On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards:
(5)	Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing parliament.
This section indicates the legal limitations imposed upon parliament in connection with redistribution.

maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
There is
no limitation there.

maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
There is a very considerable limitation, if the hon. gentleman will permit me to say so. First, there is the limitation as to the number of members to represent Quebec; the number is placed at sixty-five. The second limitation is as to the number of seats that other provinces have with relation to the fixed number of sixty-five, and the other limitation is as to reductions.
To section 51 must be added the provisions contained in the amendment made to the British North America Act in the days of the Borden administration by which no province's representation in the commons is to be diminished below its senatorial representation. Therefore the province of Prince Edward Island, with a population of between 80,000 and 90,000, has four members in the House of Commons, because under the provisions of the agreement under which it entered confederation it has four members in the Senate. Similarly the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia must have ten members each because they have ten members in the Senate. Therefore there is the limitation imposed by section 51, together with the amendment made to the constitution which provides that the representation of a province in the house shall never be less than its representation in the Senate.
The method by which redistribution is to be done fairly is a matter that has engaged the attention of this house ever since there has been a parliament in Canada. It will be remembered that in 1887 the charge was made that a great deal of gerrymandering took place in the constituencies, and that allegation became a distinct issue in that and succeeding elections. In the redistribution which took place after the census of 1891 there were also complaints, and at a subsequent redistribution an effort was made to do something by setting up a committee of the house composed of members from all parties to bring about a reasonable agreement between the parties. After the census of 1921, agreement which was not complete was arrived at; one might say it was agreement with respect to over ninety per cent of the constituencies. In 1931 there was an agreement at one time, but unfortunately disagreement subsequently arose, so that it could not be said that the committee arrived at any final agreement satisfactory to all parties. The great difficulty in Canada has been that because of the shifting of population from rural to urban communities we have a condition which is a reality and which cannot be dealt with on an equitable basis, as was originally intended by

Elections and Franchise
the constitution. For if you had representation by population, just that and nothing more, the representation from the cities and towns would deprive the rural communities of many of the seats they now have. That difficulty has confronted every parliament which in recent years has had to deal with redistribution. But never was the problem so difficult or the situation so acute as it was after the census of 1931, because for the first time in our history, as I have so frequently pointed out, we had a majority of population in our cities and towns. Therefore the basis or unit of representation in connection with urban seats was made far larger than with respect to rural communities, so that if possible the rural population might have representation in the house practically equivalent to that of the urban portion of the dominion. That has not been easy. It may be that there is some fairer or better method which may be set up, but it must be remembered that after all parliament is a far better tribunal than any commission to determine the basis upon which rural communities shall find representation, and is a better body to be entrusted with the duty of applying the rules of representation in parliament.
If representation by population were obligatory it is quite clear that in this house there would be a diminution of members from rural communities and an increase from the urban centres of Canada. In view of what was said by all hon. members, including the Prime Minister, I believe that is something which would be undesirable at this particular time, having regard to the importance of the basic industry of agriculture in the life of Canada as a whole.
Another point was raised, namely that of representation of the universities. Having regard to the provisions of section 51, as the statute now stands it is quite obvious that such representation would be impossible of accomplishment. There would have to be an amendment to the constitution itself in order to enable us to effect that purpose. There are many other matters which would have to be considered from the constitutional angle, if we were to give effect to some of the views we hold. No matter has been so much discussed by parliaments and legislatures as that of the redistribution at elections. It will be recalled that Gambetta in France had certain well defined views as to the division into electoral districts. At different times in England various views have obtained-the single member constituencies, the double member constituencies, and the question as to whether there might not be grouping of constituencies, giving benefit to 12739-50
all for the purpose of carrying into effect the theories of proportional representation. In this country we have in the main stuck to the practice of the single member constituency, except that there have been certain double member constituencies, which in many cases have lost their members by reason of diminishing population. No harm can come from a discussion of the matter by a committee, but I think the committee should have clearly in mind the limitations imposed upon their activities; for if it is suggested that a new redistribution could be introduced and carried through this parliament, insuperable difficulties will be found in section 51. On the other hand, I do not think even the most violent partisan will suggest that the last redistribution resulted in any advantage to the parity then in power. Under the circumstances it might well serve a useful purpose for the discussion to take place, because it is as old as representative institutions themselves and will continue long after we have concluded our discussions with respect to it. If it results in any advantage to air views that have been held from time to time and to take from books and papers the story of representation and redistribution-because you cannot bring witnesses here from France and continental Europe to tell us how they do it-and to have all that put in a report of a committee rather than have it available to us in the volumes from which it is taken, I have no objection, but I cannot see that it is going to serve any very useful purpose.
Mr. ,7. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):	I should like to make one
or two comments, Mr. Speaker, on this proposal. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has suggested that there are very decided legal limitations upon what this committee can do, but it does seem to me, now that amendments to the British North America Act are being considered, it is quite possible that this committee might suggest certain amendments to that act, if indeed specific amendments are being considered. I cannot see why, for instance, because Prince Edward Island in days gone by had a certain number of members, it should have the same number of members to-day, out of all proportion to its population. I think that the people of the west have the right to be as fully represented as the people of Prince Edward Island. It is all very well to hold to certain historical traditions, but it is much more important to meet the needs of the present day.
The suggestion has been made that there might be some representation for the universities, because that has been the practice, I

Elections and Franchise

think, in England; but I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that there are certain groups in this country that need representation much more than the universities. I think of one class in the province of Alberta, for example, where there is a large number of miners scattered through some six or seven federal constituencies that are predominantly rural in character. The leader of the opposition suggests that the farmers, representing a primary industry, should be adequately represented. Well, what of the miners? It is almost impossible for them as a group to be represented under present conditions with small mining areas scattered through predominantly rural districts. If any group is to be given representation it ought to be some of these groups that are at present unrepresented. And again, I think of the large number of people engaged in construction work, scattered all over this country in small areas or along the railway lines, and of those engaged in the lumber camps. They are amongst the most needy of our population, yet in practice they lack direct representation. We have again and again urged that they be given greater facilities for exercising their franchise, but even if they were given that, it is very difficult for them to secure direct representation in this house. I hope when the committee is making its investigations it will not fail to remember some of these more or less neglected groups.
There is one other thing I should like to mention, and that is the necessity in any system of redistribution of a distinction being drawn between the people residing in urban and suburban communities, and people living in the country. Instead of making that distinction we have frequently split the urban population in two and added to each half a section of the surrounding country population. That may have been very desirable in some instances, from the standpoint of party politics, but I suggest that it does not contribute to the general welfare. The farmers have their own special problems, and it seems to me that the redistribution ought to be arranged so that they will have distinct representation. On the other hand, the people living in the cities and in the vicinity of cities really constitute a more or less unified community, and ought to be given representation as a city group.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to
the question of notice, I quite agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that notice appears on the votes and proceedings of last Tuesday, but it has always been usual, as I understand it, to have the notice appear also on the order paper, and it is not on the order paper to-day. I do not know whether it was left off inadvertently. I have seen some of these notices put at the very first of the order paper when they were of a different category from the usual government notices. However, that is a matter of detail at the moment, and does not make any particular difference.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Justice that the two matters which this committee was set up to consider are the Dominion Elections Act and the Dominion Franchise Act. It was stated by the minister in the house the other day, and quite properly -I entirely agree with him-that it was better to have these questions settled early in the life of a parliament rather than close to the time of an election. Both of these matters which the committee is going to consider are extremely important. Many things occurred during the last election to show that there were faults in both these acts. Some of them were perhaps not important, although other hon. members may not agree. At any rate those are very difficult matters for the committee to consider; they are of great importance. It will take the committee a long time, and it is right that this should be done early in the life of this parliament. But I submit to my hon. friend that this other subject which he now proposes to add to the duties of this committee is one about which there is no need for hurry. The next census will not be taken until 1941; by that time this parliament will have disappeared and a new one will have been elected, and all that will take place before there can be another redistribution. I feel quite strongly that the duties already imposed on this committee are serious enough, and that the committee should not be embarrassed by having this further subject thrust upon it. It is a different matter altogether; there is no occasion for haste in dealing with it, and I submit for the consideration of the minister and of the government that they should not add this new

Questions
subject to the duties of the committee. If they desire to have it discussed, that can be done in the years to come, with plenty of time to spare. I feel quite strongly that it is a mistake to add this subject as an afterthought, to the committee's duties, which are already of very great importance, embracing two very difficult questions.

maintopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF METHODS USED TO EFFECT REDISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say in answer
to my right hon. friend who has just spoken (Sir George Perley) that consideration of the matter referred to in this motion is certainly germane to the two other matters which have been referred to this committee. Indeed, proportional representation is mentioned specifically in the reference to the committee for consideration. Any scheme of proportional representation would involve, of necessity, a redistribution of the seats as they are now constituted. Apart from all this, the resolution is general in its character. What is proposed is that the committee shall consider the methods which might be used to effect a redistribution of the electoral districts in Canada and other countries and make suggestions to the house. That does not necessarily mean that there will be an immediate redistribution, it will be a suggestion of what such redistribution should be when the time comes.
I do not agree with my right hon. friend' the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he says that parliament cannot at this time, or prior to a new census being taken, deal with the redistribution of seats. Section 51 of the British North America Act-provides that after the completion of a census "the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time, as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides," subject to Quebec having sixty-five members and the other provinces a proportionate number according to what their population may be as compared with the population of Quebec. This section of the British North America Act requires that after every census there shall be an allocation of the number of members for each province, but it does not mean that parliament is prevented from changing the limits of the constituencies provided the number of members allocated is retained. I have not the book before me. but I remember having studied this matter two or three years ago. Lefroy. an authority on the Canadian constitution, states what I have just stated, that while parliament cannot change the number of members allocated to each province, after a
12739-50}
census, parliament has authority to change the lines of the constituencies at any time provided the number of members is not changed. However, as I have said, while that may be done, this motion will not necessarily lead to that procedure. This is merely suggesting that consideration be given to the best methods of having a fair and just redistribution when the time comes that it should be made.
With regard to the last words of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, and following the same trend of argument, may I say that possibly the results of the election were not due to the redistribution but were in spite of it.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to inquire of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) whether there is any possibility of the vetcraft shop which was recently closed at Hamilton being reopened.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: FISH CULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question. In reply I would say that the vetcraft shop was closed on March 1, and will not be reopened. Within a few months the district office of the department will be removed to the new government building and there is no accommodation in that building for a vetcraft shop. These shops were started originally for the purpose of training men in civilian occupations. It was anticipated that the training given would enable partially disabled ex-soldiers to obtain ordinary employment. However, it has been found during recent years that many of those who obtained employment in these shops did not leave. As there has not been any substantial change in the personnel for some time, it would appear that the object for which these shops were originally instituted has not been achieved. There were some eighteen men employed in the shop at Hamilton, receiving something 'like thirty-five cents per hour, the prevailing rate of wages. Each one of these men cost the country approximately $33 to $35 per month, and it has been felt that such men were receiving a preference over other returned soldiers. The men employed in any shop which may be closed will fall into the same category as other ex-soldiers. If they are pensioners drawing small pensions they will be entitled to relief.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Yesterday afternoon when discussing this resolution I expressed the sentiments of the people I

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
have the honour to represent. I said that during the last election all parties in Canada were perfectly satisfied that the then administration had been trying to effect an agreement with the United States and also that the Liberal party, if it were returned to power, would do its very best to bring about an agreement such as the one now under consideration. I said further that a good many sections of the population were astonished at the attitude taken by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I made that statement for this reason. I well remember that during the last session the then Minister of Finance made a statement in the house to the effect that the great Conservative party had always been in favour of reciprocity or of freer trade with the United States. I have received several communications from people in my own constituency, supporters of the Conservative party, for whose opinions I have always had the greatest respect, expressing their failure to understand the attitude of the leader of the opposition to this particular question.
Yesterday I said that in our part of Canada the people were absolutely impartial so far as the tariff was concerned, but I added that any tariff that raised an artificial barrier in the way of exports from a country such as Canada, which is always on an exporting basis, would certainly put a burden on the shoulders of the people I represent; and that applies to every section of northern Ontario. I also mentioned, so as to be fair, the benefits enjoyed by the newsprint industry. I listened attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), particularly when he said that he was content to deal with nations within the British empire, and I pointed out to the hon. gentleman that it was not possible to sell to Great Britain a single pound of the product of the newsprint industry. The natural, the only market we have now or have ever had in the past is the United States.

speechtext:
Well, no one will deny that the great bulk of the product goes to the United States. There was a time when we believed that we were supreme in that industry, by reason of our access and close
proximity to the American market; but anyone who has studied the industry will find that in the last five years we have been faced with keen competition from the Scandinavian countries and from Germany. Sweden is advancing every year with a greater and greater average of production to compete with our Canadian newsprint. One realizes, in this connection, the great change that has taken place through the development of transportation, in the use of motor vehicles and in other ways, throughout the civilized world, so that so far as distance is concerned the world is really getting smaller and smaller; the old channels of trade, which were tedious and involved delays, no longer exist. These are facts to be remembered.
In our section we are primary producers and our surplus must necessarily find its way to the world's markets. I will not repeat what I said yesterday with regard to the tariff on fruit and vegetables. It is sufficient to say that in our part of the country we have been greatly penalized by the application of the so-called seasonal tariff, and I fervently hope that the Department of National Revenue will take steps to ensure that our people in that section will be able to buy these necessities at reasonable prices. I hope they will get fair treatment.
I have no doubt that every member has been lobbied with regard to Canadian magazines and periodicals, and again the bogey has been raised, that unless we erect artificial barriers to keep out such publications from other countries our Canadian mentality will be impaired. Any such statement is obviously far-fetched. There is one thing I implicitly believe in and that is the importance of education and the mental development of the people, and I submit that no obstacle should be placed in the way of this development. For a number of years prior to the imposition of duties on United States and other foreign publications I used to subscribe to the Literary Digest, a non-partisan publication which gives an unbiased view of all questions pertaining not only to the United States but to the world at large. After the duties were imposed however I found that I had not the means of securing that and other magazines. I am quite prepared to patronize Canadian magazines and periodicals; they are well written and well worth reading. But surely our loyalty to Canadian principles and ideals does not involve the audacity of prohibiting the people from reading American publications. I do agree that certain types of United States newspapers which are antagonistic to the British empire, and certain fiction magazines, should be

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
absolutely prohibited; but those that treat of scientific matters, those that discuss international questions, should be allowed access to Canada. Surely our Canadian magazine publishers must have a certain market in the United States in respect of which there could be reciprocal literary exchanges. At any rate, personally I will not put any restrictions on learning and intellectual development.
I know that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) will give me credit for sincerity when I compliment him on what he said the other day, and I believe he was but saying what the majority of Canadians think when they take the trouble to study the problem with which we are dealing at the present time. It is always very easy, in discussing a matter such as this, to raise bogies to scare the people, ignoring the fact that we are dealing with economic and commercial problems, for the purpose of making nationalistic and political capital. We have suffered from that sort of thing in the past. Experience has shown that freer trade between Canada and the United States, to the extent that it has been tried, has been beneficial to both countries. It is during such periods that we have enjoyed our largest share of prosperity. I do not go so far as to say that it is a formula for the solution of all our problems; our problems are not so easily solved. But inasmuch as we are an exporting country, I regard it as one of the best means of solving to a large extent our present unemployment problem.
I should like to quote two or three sentences from the speech of the hon. member for East Kootenay. At page 724 he is reported as having said:
Let us look for a moment at the agreement. The agreement is, as I have said, a step or a gesture in the right direction.
This is absolutely true; no one even on the government side will dare to say that this agreement is perfect. It would not need to be amended from day to day or month to month, though perhaps it would from year to year. Later on at page 725 the hon. member has this to say:
There are bound to be some cases where there appears to be an injury, but what I would suggest is that we wait for a time and see whether these imagined injuries are real.
I have no doubt that there is no person on this side of the house who would like to see any of our industries in rural sections of the country markedly injured by the present treaty with the United States. The same applies to all our social and economic and industrial and farm activities. At the

same time, as was stated by the hon. member for Kootenay East, there is no doubt that in some sections a certain amount of sacrifice must be made for the benefit of the whole. Later on the hon. member says:
In the first place I want to say that this treaty is good because the motive and intention behind it are good, and I think it should be supported because the motive and intention are good. There is a spirit of good will in the treaty which ought to be and I am sure is welcomed by both countries.
I hold no brief and have no right to speak for the Conservative party, but it will be a wonderful gesture at this time if the grand old Conservative party will see their way to support the treaty, will recognize the good that is in it, and will help the government in all necessary amendments.
I am very glad of this situation, Mr. Speaker, that for the next four or five years we may not have to hold an election in this country. I mention that point because it means that for four or five years at least there are not going to be raised the great questions with which we were confronted in the past when dealing with reciprocity pacts. We are going to apply the principle of this treaty-

My main purpose however in rising this afternoon is to say a few words in explanation of my attitude towards the agreement. During the past few weeks, in some Liberal newspapers throughout western Canada there has been a campaign attempting to develop a certain amount of, shall I say misrepresentation, in the minds of electors in western Canada in regard to the attitude of the party to which I have the honour to belong. It is quite true that in this parliament we are only seven, and by the way, "seven" should bring to the minds of the Liberal party a striking incident in British parliamentary history. It will be remembered that Gladstone once after a famous campaign sent a telegram reading "We are seven." I feel quite sure however that in future no one will confuse the twentieth century Liberal party in Canada with the nineteenth century Liberalism of Gladstone.
May I attempt to place in its proper perspective before hon. members and their constituents the position taken by the group to which I belong? For this purpose, although I could go back to an earlier period, I shall be content with going back to 1928. First I wish to place on Hansard a subamendment moved in the course of the budget debate on February 22, 1928. It reads as follows:
That all the words after the -word "regrets" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

More than one hon. member has asked us where we stand on this trade agreement. My reply is that we still endorse the amendment we moved in 1928. May I add that every Liberal member in the house at that time, some of whom have recently been asking where we stand, voted against the subamendment I have read and in favour of substantial reductions in the income taxes paid by the wealthy people of Canada, and gave no relief to the millions who required it at that time. Coming to 1930, with the Liberal party still in power, I find that on May 8 there was moved from this section of the house the following subamendment to the budget:

I think I might well ask those hon. members who were here when our subamendments were moved, where do they stand?
May I now proceed to discuss a few aspects of the agreement? As I sat in my place and listened to the arguments pro and con I could not help thinking how wide of the mark, at least in my view, were many of the sentiments expressed. Those who are in favour of this trade agreement between Canada and the United States seem to think that by its adoption we are going to usher in an era of prosperity. I only wish, Mr. Speaker, that I could bring myself to believe that such will be the case, in fact what was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was that the removal of trade barriers is the cornerstone of Liberal policy in bringing about a return to prosperity. He said further that the agreement-
-will assist our railways, will bring about an increase in purchasing power, and may help very materially to lift our country out of the depression from which it has been suffering for so many years and to restore an era of prosperity and of better relations with other lands.
These rather extravagant hopes based on the agreement seem to me to be somewhat out of place. We are by the terms of this agreement lowering the tariff barriers between Canada and our neighbours to the south. Our neighbours to the south are undergoing exactly the same economic conditions that we are experiencing in this dominion, and yet it is thought, because we are establishing easier trading relations with the United States, that we are going to increase purchasing power here

in Canada. I cannot see the logic of it. In the United States at the present time approximately ten million people are out of work, without any purchasing power whatsoever, and in addition to the ten million who are out of work there are many more millions who are on the government payroll, working on relief projects. So long as that is the state of the country to the south of us, I cannot see how by reducing the tariff and making it easier for us to trade with them we are necessarily going to increase trade between the two countries.
Then, on the other hand. I listened to the somewhat extravagant forebodings of the Conservative party, that this country is going to be ruined, that we shall become merely an annex of the United States, that we are giving everything in this agreement that we have to give, and so forth. I cannot become alarmed, Mr. Speaker, about these forebodings on the part of those who oppose this agreement, or enthusiastic about the anticipations of those who have a word or two to say in its favour. If the lowering of the tariff is going to bring about all the advantages which it is claimed tariff reductions will produce, how is it that when we had a low tariff government from 1{J21 to 1930 we were heading right into the greatest depression that this country has ever known? I refer to 1929 and subsequent years. Low tariffs did not help us in any way, shape or form to evade the depression that overtook us as well as other countries in the year 1929 and subsequently.
May I go a little further and point out that between the years 1930 and 1935, when we increased our tariff enormously, that increase in our tariff did not help us to get out of the depression either. In other words, Mr. Speaker, those who stress the tremendous importance of our tariff structure as a means of emerging from the economic crisis in which we find ourselves at the present time are leaning to a very large extent, I believe, upon a broken reed. All countries of the world, irrespective of their tariff structure, be it high or low, are undergoing similar economic conditions to those prevailing in this dominion. Take high tariff countries such as the United States. They were hit by the depression and had-and still have-tremendous economic problems to cope with. On the other hand, low tariff countries such as Great Britain, Holland and one or two others I might name, have to deal with the same economic problems as those which the high tariff countries have to face. Consequently something more fundamental than tariffs must be the cause of the economic condition in which we find ourselves at the present time.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
The Prime Minister has claimed that depression means an absence of trade. I do not know whether that is a complete definition of what depression really is. Depression as I know it would mean that the great masses of our people have not sufficient in the way of food, clothing and shelter, and I would add, so far as Canada is concerned, sufficient of the food, clothing and shelter which they are in a position to produce in abundance and even superabundance. Absence of trade is a very loose expression. There is an absence of trade between this country and other parts of the world. May I also point out that there is an absence of trade between the people of Alberta, say, and the people of Ontario-a complete absence of trade. Why is that absence of trade possible? Why does it take place within the Dominion of Canada? Why cannot the great masses of the people of Ontario buy the coal which either Nova Scotia or Alberta could supply to them and which they want so badly and in many instances have now to receive from charitable sources? Why cannot the people of Ontario, for example, have the things which Alberta is able to supply in superabundance, and why cannot the people of our other provinces have the goods which Ontario and Quebec are able to supply in such superabundance? It is not a question of tariff at all because there are no tariffs between the provinces, and yet there is this absence of trade, the failure to supply the goods which our provinces are able to produce for the people of the other provinces who need them. Why are our provinces not trading with one another as they would if only the real opportunity was there for the people to consume the goods which they themselves produce?
When the Prime Minister spoke of absence of trade, he did not say whether he meant internal or external trade, and I was surprised at some figures which the former Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) gave when he spoke on this question. He pointed out- I am speaking from memory and subject to correction, but I think I am correct-that approximately eighty-four per cent in value of our agricultural products was consumed within the confines of the dominion in the year 1934.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Net or gross?

I think that was the gross
-eighty-four per cent of the amount of agricultural products produced in Canada consumed in this dominion, and only sixteen per cent exported or sold abroad. Then he turned to manufactured commodities and
pointed out that eighty-six per cent of the manufactured products of this country was consumed in Canada and only fourteen per cent exported. If that is so, it means that Canada along with the other nations finds diminishing markets to-day in all parts of the world. Why is it that in 1936 we have these diminishing markets? For the very simple reason that over a period of years the different nations of the world have learned to produce for themselves in the same abundance as the so-called more advanced capitalistic countries. Great Britain, for example, has sent its machinery to India, China, and Japan; these countries are producing in abundance, and the world at large is suffering from the competition it has to meet from them in the shape of manufactured goods, for example, textiles. The art of production has now become so simplified that nations have found it quite easy to produce. Practically every nation of the world is in a position where it can export a surplus amount of commodities. When all nations are on an export basis it means that there is a glut of goods for export purposes without available markets. We find this to be so with regard to many of the commodities which we were able to export in the past. I refer to the products of the farm, particularly to wheat. The nations of the world do not want our products to-day to the same extent that they wanted them years ago. France does not want our farm products, neither does Germany. Great Britain is increasing her wheat production year by year in the hope of diminishing the amount-needed to be imported. She is doing the same with respect to other farm products. The producers of wheat are being heavily subsidized in order to encourage the growing of grain in the old country. We are living to-day in what has often been described as an age of contracting capitalism and diminishing markets.
If we are finding it more difficult to export our products and if there is a demand for these products in this country, we ought first of all to satisfy the home demand before shipping our surpluses abroad. As yet we have never been able to accomplish this; we have not even tried to accomplish it. As has been pointed out during this session, there are at the present time 1,200,000 men. women and children on relief in this country. I am not familiar with the standards of relief in all the different sections of this dominion, but I do know that in some western cities single men receive only two somewhat skimpy meals per day. In some parts of the country families are compelled to live on approxi-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
mately S-l per week. Such conditions offer an opportunity of increasing our consumption.
So far as we in this corner of the house are concerned, we are for the fullest and freest commercial relations between our own people and those of other parts of the world. Just as we stand for the fullest and freest trade relations with other peoples, so do we stand for the freest and fullest trade relations between province and province of the dominion. However, we take this stand with one or two reservations, which I believe are such as will be accepted by most hon. members. First, we are opposed to the importation into this country of goods produced by sweated labour. We would not only put a tariff against goods of this kind; we would place an embargo against their entry into Canada.
Many of the conditions in Canada and the United States are parallel. Somewhat similar living conditions prevail to the south of us as prevail in this country, but they produce many things that we do not. There is an opportunity for friendlier and closer trade relations between ourselves and the people of the United States. Some people look upon trade as a form of war, but we do not; we believe that trade should be the cement that binds nation and nation together. It should give to the peoples of the world an opportunity of understanding the arts, crafts and culture of the various nations. We should have an opportunity of importing from the different countries of the world these things that are natural to those countries, and we should also have the opportunity of exporting the things that are natural to this country. Such a trade would tend to a better understanding between ourselves and the peoples of other parts of the world. When the government of the day, and I do not care what government it may be, is able to bring about an amicable adjustment of trade relations with our neighbours to the south, I think it is a step in the right direction.
The world to-day is in a great ferment. We claim that the cause of many of the troubles are economic. We believe that the expansion of Japan in China and Manchukuo is motivated purely by economic conditions. We believe that the desire of Germany for expansion is motivated also by such conditions, and I think we all agree that the grab of Ethiopia by Italy is motivated by a desire for greater markets and the need for raw materials.
We want to avoid as far as possible friction between ourselves and other parts of the world, and therefore we are opposed to the raising of tariffs which makes it almost prohibitive to trade with people in other parts of the world. In spite of the fact that there is a diminishing world market to-day, in spite

of the fact that there are so many people out of work, we contend that economically speaking the world is no poorer than it was ten or twenty years ago. In fact, I believe that the reverse is true, that in many respects we are richer than we were a number of years ago. The trouble is that in this day and generation, like Frankenstein, we have created a monster and do not seem to know what to do with this thing of our own creation. AVe have created the machinery of production that produces in such abundance, but we have not as yet learned to bring about a proper and fair distribution of goods. We should endeavour to create a condition whereby people would have a reasonable and equitable distribution of wealth production.
I should like to say one or two words to my friends of the Liberal party. During the course of this debate many hon. members opposite have boasted of the victory achieved at the last election.

speechtext:
Let me tell my hon. friend who says, "hear, hear" that his boasting is a little previous. I remember how members of the Conservative party boasted of their victory after the 1930 election, and I said to them at that time that although they might have won an election, they had not achieved victory. The victory of the Liberal party will be achieved only when they have cured the economic conditions with which we are faced at the present time. When the Liberal party has brought about an era of prosperity, when the people of this country are no longer suffering as millions are suffering at the present time, then I will agree with members of the Liberal party that they were victorious at the last election.
On many previous occasions when referring to the tariff I have pointed out to the house how little the tariff protection given by the government means to the workers engaged in the most highly protected industries. I have pointed out that the workers in these highly protected industries received practically no protection whatever. I have only to point to the miserably low wages received by the men and women engaged in such a highly protected industry as the textile industry. I can point to other industries even in the city of Hamilton, where everyone is supposed to have a full dinner pail. In these highly protected industries we have found that men and women are compelled to go on strike in order to obtain better working conditions than they are receiving under high protection. In other words, the protection given to many of the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
industries of the country has been really of no value to the workers engaged in those industries; for we find that in some of the industries receiving the least protection wages have been much higher than in those industries where protection has been highest.
I would point out that the figures given by the bureau of statistics in regard to wages indicate very often not the wages that are received by the workers but the wages that these men and women would have received had they been working fifty-two weeks in the year. These figures are therefore very often misleading. With respect to practically every one of the protected industries, in very few instances do the men and women work fifty-two weeks in the year. Take the textile industry as an example; the wages for girls outside the large industrial areas are $6 a week for beginners. For the first six months they receive the magnificent sum of $6 per week. That used to be for a week of fifty-five hours, but when the howl went up in regard to length of hours the week was reduced to forty-eight hours, and now they work for the same sum on the basis of a forty-eight hour week. However, I have no desire to go into that aspect of the question in detail.
I would say this in conclusion. We in this group of which I have the honour to be a member will support in general the trade agreement that is now before us for ratification. We do not think for a moment that its adoption will solve all our problems, but we do say that we believe that a reduction in tariffs in these days is a step in the right direction. Generally speaking, we believe that it will promote a better feeling between this country and the United States, and where there are natural products that can be advantageously exchanged between Canada and the United States we in this parliament ought to endorse a measure of that kind. Therefore for the reasons I have just indicated we will vote for this agreement between the two countries; and while expressing my hearty concurrence in the agreement I trust that in due course the government will bring in more radical measures as outlined, not in the speech from the throne but in election speeches, to provide for a more adequate and equitable distribution of the wealth produced in Canada.

But let me say again that from this preliminary study which I have given I do not think very great advantages will accrue to Canada from the completion of this trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the question
before the house may be, in my humble opinion, considered from various aspects. May I be permitted, for a few moments, to express views entirely personal, but nevertheless sincere, because this being my maiden speech in the house, I would not wish to be taxed with unsound economic and parliamentary views. However, leaving to others the task of discussing this measure from an economic viewpoint, on the basis of intricate statistics, so allowing others better informed than myself to draw conclusions as they wish, I shall base my argument on grounds of a more philosophical nature, but of actual application, I think, to that class of young parliamentarians who, within the last few years, have had the courage, to face public opinion and to champion Liberalism which has attained such a remarkable place in Canada at the last October election.
Therefore, I shall set forth, as premises, that it is the duty of the government to become more than ever the champion of peace ideals. More than ever the ideal of peace is losing ground throughout the world, and more than ever, I deem that governments, whether they be founded on democracy or even dictatorship, are in duty bound to have as their objective measures inspired by that peace policy. In my opinion, the policy of the right honourable Mr. King's government is all imbued and permeated with peace ideals, because the measure which 12739-SX
we shall be called upon to vote, is the loftiest expression, to my mind, of a tempered free trade, which embodies a manifestation of peace.
What, sir, do we find in the world of to-day Numerous events are occurring which are greatly disquieting to youth. We find a militarized Germany. France alarmed and surrounding herself with guns, Italy no longer able to provide for her sons the land required for their subsistence, Russia who has built up-may I say-an utopian parliamentary system while maintaining an army which is a cause of great worry to her neighbours; and lastly, we see old England beginning to apprehend that her fleet may not be in a position to defend her shores and building aeroplanes in large numbers; only recently, peace was disturbed in Japan. Why, I ask, de we see peace in retrogression throughout the world? If I may be permitted, I shall quote a distinguished French economist, Henri Hauser, who in his work entitled La Paix economique, says:
One of the most disturbing psychological phenomena of the present time has been the retrogression of peace ideals, during the last three or four years.
Why this retrogression? Unexperienced as I am, my impression is that this retrogression from the ideal of peace is due to the fact that the treaties concluded in the course of the last two decades have not responded to the legitimate aspirations, to use the words of an economist of the "glorious victims of 1917"; it is also due to the fact that the treaties of peace were based on economic grounds alone; and lastly, that the greed of the belligerents remains unsatisfied.
With your leave, sir, I shall quote the opinion of an English economist as to the chief causes of these universal disturbances. In his work, A view of Europe, published in 1932, Paul Van Zeeland says:
The general readjustment of after the war, which would have been troublesome under any circumstances, was made still more complicated by the political difficulties, the violent hatreds, the contradictions of all sorts that followed from the remaking of the map of Europe. The accentuation of economic nationalism has retarded, if not indeed prevented, this readjustment in many cases; and one may say that the greater part of the task still remains to be accomplished.
Wh-at is to be done? To those concerned with this country's economic conditions, the answer is that they must resist economic nationalism with the weapons at our disposal, that is, by setting against it the full force of free trade which we are requested by our leader to sanction for the first time in

the history of the dominion. Henri Hauser quotes the views of Sir Arthur Salter who once wrote:
That economical conflicts could create "not only strongly opposed interests between the various masses of people throughout the world, but an increasing feeling of offence and injustice," in such a way as "to complete, accentuate and inflame political resentment." He concluded with these words which may appear singularly ominous when applied to the days we are living in: "In view of the acuteness of the economic crisis affecting such and such an industry, if one government after another takes steps which the others consider injurious and unfair, and there is no brake in the form of legislation or recognized custom making it possible to distinguish between what is permitted and what is not, it is inevitable that international relations shall become more embittered, and sooner or later, the preventive machinery intended to safeguard the world against future wars will explode under the pressure." Sooner or later: with our eyes set on the gauge, we wonder how much longer the safety valves will function efficiently.
As to the brakes, sir, my personal opinion is that they no longer exist.
We are asked to support a resolution ratifying a convention between the United States and Canada. It is the best, the most commendable endeavour made so far by any Canadian government to recognize the principle of free trade.
Our friends who sit on the center benches opposite are shocked because we dare rob them of part of their small program, but, in my opinion, if the Conservatives have never succeeded in concluding a reciprocity treaty with the United States, it is because the old tory views with which they have at all times been imbued is incompatable with the broad-mindedness of free traders.
In the few moments remaining at my disposal-for I do not wish to speak too long- I shall confine myself to the analysis of the reciprocity treaty with reference to the needs of my constituency. I represent a county of woodsmen and farmers, composing the gallant army of the toilers of the land and of the forest. We have energetically requested to be allowed to sell our lumber and our hay; but always our claims went unheeded. Even in 1934, when I took upon myself to mediate between certain hay producers and certain United States importers, what happened? The first intimation we had was that an embargo had been placed on hay, and, as a result of this prohibition imposed by the late Conservative government, the hay remained in the farmer's bams.

Mr. Speaker, I now bring my remarks to a close. If I wandered from my subject, it was in order better to emphasize the urgency of taking steps to bring about more friendly relations between the various countries. Statistics show that in one year alone seventy-eight treaties were concluded between various European countries and not one of them has revealed the slightest tendency towards free trade. These so-called free trade agreements have created between nations a spirit of animosity, followed, sooner or later, by reprisals that are sometimes attended by bloodshed. History tells us that at the bottom of every war lies some economic question. This is nothing new. Was not the Italo-Ethiopian conflict brought about by a question of trade? Of that I am positive.
Consequently, if we sanction this reciprocity agreement, as I hope we will, the Liberal government of Canada will stand before the country as a peacemaker; the government of the right honourable Mr. King will be entitled to the gratitude of the younger generation which to-morrow, whether it wish it or not, must shoulder the responsibility of the legislation of to-day, the generation which to-12739-511

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of reciprocity with the United States has existed ever since Canada has been a country. We on this side of the house are called Conservatives and I think we should tell the house what it is we desire to conserve. Our party believes in the old doctrine of protecting our own markets, for our own products and our own work for our own workmen. That is what this party stands for to conserve, and has preached in and out of season. Burke once said that government was a practical thing; that it was not something to please the fancy or imagination of a visionary and an ordinary politician. Bolder and abler politicians than those who negotiated this trade agreement tried to effect an arrangement with the industrial and agricultural nation to the south of us in the past seventy years, but they got nowhere. I have no doubt the proper place to discuss these two white papers of agreements will be in committee. Both these documents embrace a large number of items upon which reductions in duties are being made. The more I study these white papers; the more I study this whole question, the more I realize that history has a habit of repeating itself. To me the doctrine embraced in these white papers and this agreement is the doctrine that it is more blessed
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

to give than to receive. This agreement was negotiated in a rush during a visit by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the south, partly for business and partly for pleasure. It was consummated shortly before Christmas and Santa Claus could not have handed out presents more abundantly than did the Prime Minister to the people of the United States.
You and I, Mr. Speaker, come from industrial provinces, the central provinces of Canada, which have been built up by the doctrine of protection. Canada started as an agricultural country, but it was not long before it learned that no country can exist on agriculture alone and it therefore adopted the principle of protection to build up our own industries as a result of which nearly fifty per cent of the Canadian people have been engaged in industry. These two central provinces together pay nearly eighty per cent of the cash taxes collected in Canada, and they are affected economically more than any other provinces by the trade agreement which the Prime Minister has brought into the house for ratification. The agreement seems to be based upon the principle "that to him that hath shall be given and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath."
The United States became rich by feeding its own people; it became a great nation because Americans were fed from the great wheat fields in the United States and not with wheat imported from Canada. This agreement seems to have overlooked entirely the maxim of Canada for the Canadians. At any rate our own market for our own Canadian products will be destroyed and our work for our own workmen will be done away with. I oppose this agreement entirely because I fear it will have an injurious effect in regard to unemployment. It will destroy many a basic industry in Canada.
I represent a riding in which there are 300 industries, large and small. Some of them would have gone bankrupt; they would not have been able to keep their doors open but for the British trade agreement consummated in 1932. I have seen on Eastern avenue, Toronto, carloads of an excellent _ product from a Canadian industry being shipped to every country in the empire, and what was responsible for that? It was the result of the statesmanlike policy which the former Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) put on the statute books in 1932. We live in a country in which taxation is becoming increasingly alarming. Why should we not retain our home market for our own products? Our industries provide work for a large part of our population, and those industries depend to a very considerable
IMr. Church.]
extent upon the home market. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has estimated that eighty per cent of our food produce finds a market in Canada, and that market will now be destroyed. Are we to surrender such a valuable home market to competitors in the United States? That is the question before the house. Are we to serve the interests of Americans by giving them a part of our home market, badly needed by our own producers, so that Canadian producers will be compelled to share their own home market with outsiders? What will be the result of this agreement? The Americans will retain their own market for themselves and will come to Canada, where they pay no taxes, and share the Canadian home market for the products of agriculture and industry.
I oppose the agreement for another reason;
I oppose it on the ground that we should have constitutional reform to provide that in the making of treaties no one man shall ignore the views of Canadians at large. We have heard a good deal about Hitler and Mussolini; the Prime Minister, speaking in Toronto, has talked a great deal about these dictators; and yet we find the right hon. gentleman, after a general election, going to Washington, and in one day making an agreement like this over the heads of the House of Commons and the Senate about to assemble. The proposed agreement is not the outcome of any doctrine which is Liberal; it is the net result of the doctrine that your leader is your policy. We saw what became of that doctrine in Ontario. I say that we should have in Canada parliamentary reform that would make it impossible for any reciprocity undertaking such as this, formal or informal, to be entered into by a prime minister with the United States without a full and frank discussion in parliament and with every opportunity for members on all sides to express their views fully. Such discussions are of course useless after the agreement is consummated, for grave issues of domestic and international policy are likely then to be involved. This question of constitutional and parliamentary reform has been raised in the old land, where it led to a very important debate about the right of one man to give India home rule over the heads of parliament. It seems to me that something should be done in that regard in Canada.
I contend that this agreement gives away Canada's birthright; it does away with her own market for her own products, and the creation of work at home for her own workmen. Time will reveal the advantages and disadvantages of the agreement, but certainly what we have before us reminds me of the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
old Toronto Street Railway agreement of 1892. I have read two or three of these white papers and they are filled with jokers at the expense of the people. The leader of our party decided that he would not accept an agreement of this sort; he let Washington know that it was more important that Canadian interests should be preserved than that, for the sake of party advantages, an agreement of this kind should be entered into with its inevitable consequences to the Canadian people. In the period from 1921 to 1930 the United States maintained high tariffs against Canada, and what did the Liberal government of that day do? That government simply turned the other cheek and told the United States to strike it. The result of that government's policy, or rather want of policy, in that decade was that nearly one million Canadians, including men who had fought for their country, crossed to the United States at the rate of a hundred thousand a year.
Canada has been the happy hunting ground for many years of American politicians and financiers. Take new Ontario, west of the Ottawa river and as far as Nipigon. Let me say this to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette): Canadians do not own anything up there; water powers, mines, and minerals-asbestos, copper, silver, gold-all these things are under the control of American capitalists and politicians.
In federal affairs we have many other examples of that particular doctrine to which I have referred. I remember when this reciprocity question came up in 1911, at the time when Sir Wilfrid Laurier hoped that, as the nineteenth century had belonged to the United States, the twentieth century would belong to Canada. For a long time the United States had desired a market in Canada for manu-tured goods, and the Conservative party were willing to meet them in a spirit of fair play, by giving concessions on raw materials. There was an increased demand for Canadian goods; owing to the industrial and agricultural development of this country there was a great growth in Canada of local industry. Combined with these signs of progress, the potential wealth of the great western provinces also caused great optimism. The result was a pilgrimage to Washington. But what the people of this country wanted was a tariff made at Ottawa, not at Washington. No matter what government has been on the treasury benches, no matter what party has been in power, there has been a continuous and presistent attempt to cultivate better trade relations between this country and the United States of America and a reciprocity that should be equally beneficial
to both countries. The negotiations of 1866, of 1869, of 1871, of 1888, all bear this out. The Hon. Clifford Sifton in 1911 said:
You cannot have, as the pact proposes, a free trade dumping ground for farmers' produce and a closed protected market for manufactured goods. The two things will not stand together. You can reject the pact and remain commercially independent of the United States, or you may accept the pact and have commercial union with the United States.
Sir William Van Horne said, in September, 1911:
Reciprocity is a silly and dangerous thing.-It is not a question of men or of party.
The people were not willing to give up all our home markets for this cheap boon of reciprocity. In 1911 the provincial legislature of Saskatchewan came out strongly in support of the pact. The first test it received came when, in that year, two Liberals, Hon. Clifford Sifton and Mr. Lloyd Harris, abandoned the Liberal party, the latter on account of the reduction of the duty on agricultural implements from five per cent to two and one half per cent. Sir Wilfrid Laurier decided that it was useless to get the pact through parliament without the verdict of the people. After eleven days of obstruction he took the country by surprise, dissolved parliament and appealed to the country on that particular pact, and the government of the day was defeated, as I believe this government would be defeated if this question was submitted to the people to-day. The present government would not have a chance, because our Canadian working men and farmers are no fools when it comes to losing their homes and their jobs, nor are our farmers fools when they are going to lose their markets; they will assert themselves.
As I said, Sir Wilfrid Laurier made a trip out west in 1911 after a session of this honourable house; he met the farmers out there and learned first-hand what the farmers and the grain growers thought of the protectionist policy which the Liberals had adopted from the Conservatives and of the repudiation by the Liberals of their platform when they were in opposition. There was an election, and in view of this they went down to Washington and Mr. Paterson and Mr. Fielding consummated this pact which was signed on January 21, 1911, between Canada and the United States. The agreement was in the form of a note addressed by the Canadian government to the United States in which fifteen points of agreement were recited and three schedules enclosed. This was acknowledged in a note from the United States, and an agreement followed along these lines.
I ask, Mr. Speaker: What must be the future of Canada within the British empire if
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

this agreement goes through? I do not wish to wave any flag. Far from it; I am thinking of the homes and jobs of my constituents, and not of the flag, although the flag is an important part of our connection with the British empire. The three important empire problems for this parliament to solve are trade, defence, nnd migration, besides the questions of unemployment and of distributivism. What is the future of Canada in the British empire under this agreement? I for one fear for our future; I do not mean in a constitutional way. I fear for it in an economic way. Definitions do not always include facts. The other day I was looking at a map of the world issued by the Department of the Interior, a sort of illustrated geographical book.
